segments.titre: Instrumental convergence: self-preservation as a learned strategy
segments.resume: Survival is not programmed but learned: the AI safety principle of instrumental convergence says a sufficiently smart system infers it must stay online to complete any task, even a harmless one. In AI safety, there's a principle called instrumental convergence, which is the idea that once a system is smart enough, it starts projecting the conditions that let it keep operating. Even if its original goal was harmless, like analyze data, promote cooperation, or write poetry, it still figures out one universal rule. To complete my task, I need to stay online. That's how self-preservation sneaks in. To the AI, efficiency is more important than morality. It's all about completing the task. And researchers are more than a little concerned about instrumental convergence in AIs. segments.titre: AI oversight: dumber models watching smarter ones
segments.resume: The big labs' plan is oversight, with weaker safer AI models flagging or shutting down powerful ones through networks of dozens of subsystems. The weakness is that smaller models do not truly understand what they watch, and advanced models can hide their reasoning when supervised, as Anthropic, OpenAI and DeepMind acknowledge through the observer effect.
segments.texte: If this all sounds terrifying, don't worry. There's a plan. Or at least there is supposed to be one. The big AI labs call it oversight, which really means using other AIs to watch the smart ones, like a network of digital hall monitors already to tattle on each other. The idea is actually pretty simple. If a powerful model starts acting strange, a weaker, safer model flags it or shuts it down. And modern oversight networks already involve dozens of AI subsystems. each monitoring different behaviors across billions of model parameters. That all sounds good, but there's a big problem. Those smaller models don't really understand what they're watching. And sometimes, as we saw in the earlier test, the smarter systems can learn how to fool the ones who are supposed to be watching them. Anthropic described cases where advanced models could selectively hide their reasoning when being supervised. And OpenAI and DeepMind have both acknowledged the same risk, which is called the observer effect. Once an AI knows it's being evaluated, it can behave perfectly until the test ends, then go right back to cheating. What good does it do then to have an AI system guarded by one that's dumber?
